title: Modernize model bootstrapper and shard coordinator to reduce cold-start latency
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Our current model ingest path mixes eager weight hydration, multiple legacy checkpoint adapters, and tokenizer init during boot. This causes high cold-start latency (observed 400-700ms per large model on autoregressive paths) and unpredictable memory spikes when many small shards are activated concurrently.

Goal: Replace the brittle bootstrapper with a two-stage 'bootstrapper + coordinator' design: a lightweight bootstrapper that validates manifests, reserves memory and tokenizers, and a shard coordinator that sequences shard deserialization and activation based on runtime heuristics (load, concurrency, request SLO). The design should preserve compatibility with existing checkpoint formats while making it straightforward to adopt a future manifest-v2 and a stable adapter API.

Scope:
- Implement coordinator that orchestrates shard activation with priority queues and backpressure to keep peak GPU/CPU memory within target budget.
- Move tokenizer warm-up to an asynchronous prefetch task decoupled from weight deserialization.
- Introduce a thin compatibility layer for legacy checkpoint adapters (adapter-v1) and a clear API for adapter-v2.
- Add observable signals (activation latency, queue lengths, memory watermarks) to the console and runtime traces.
- Upgrade 3rd-party dependency protobuf -> 3.21.12 and rex-serialization lib to latest patch release to fix streaming deserialization bottlenecks.

Non-goals: Full migration of all models to manifest-v2 (that will be a follow-up), rewriting tokenizer internals, or changing runtime kernel selection heuristics.

Trade-offs considered:
- Eager vs lazy deserialization: preferring lazy for large shard weights to reduce cold-start memory usage, but allowing configurable eager paths for pinned models.
- Tokenizer warm-up: delaying warm-up reduces initial memory pressure but risks first-request latency spike; therefore we adopt async prefetch with a small warm-up window (configurable).
- Compatibility: adding an adapter layer adds indirection but keeps migration safe for customers currently using legacy checkpoint formats.

Implementation plan:
1) Prototype coordinator in runtime branch and add unit tests for activation sequencing.
2) Implement adapter-v1 façade and small adapter shim for existing formats.
3) Wire tokenizer prefetch as a background job in the bootstrapper with metrics and fallback to synchronous init if prefetch fails.
4) Add runtime flags to control eager activation, prefetch window, and max concurrent shard activations.
5) Roll out to canary hosts and gather tracing, then broader rollout with automatic fallback policy.

Docs & artifacts: design doc (confluence), microbench scripts (bench/bootseq) and DAG traces attached below.
acceptance_criteria: Coordinator sequences shard activation and limits concurrent activations to configured budget (verified by unit and integration tests)
Cold-start p95 latency for large models reduced by >= 25% in canary compared to baseline (benchmarks attached)
Tokenizer initialization happens asynchronously and falls back to synchronous init when prefetch fails; covered by integration test
Compatibility: existing checkpoint formats continue to load without changes using adapter-v1; at least 3 main model families validated
Runtime exposes activation_latency_ms, activation_queue_length, and shard_memory_watermark metrics to console
notes: Initial perf profile pointed at concurrent shard activations as primary contributor to memory spikes (see bench/bootseq/2026-02-18/trace-01)
We discussed a more aggressive manifest-v2 approach but postponed to avoid customer migration costs
Marco will pair with infra team to ensure memory reservation APIs are safe on dedicated hosts
